prescriptions.name: Acne Vulgaris
prescriptions.summary: Acne vulgaris is a common chronic inflammatory skin condition involving the pilosebaceous units. It commonly presents with comedones, papules, pustules, nodules, and scarring, often on the face, chest, and back. Treatment is tailored to severity and may include topical agents, oral antibiotics, and adjunctive skincare.

prescriptions.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule once daily with food for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Azelaic Acid 15% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas twice daily for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Benzoyl Peroxide 2.5% gel
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected areas at bedtime for 12 weeks

prescriptions.name: Acne Soap (salicylic acid based)
prescriptions.sig: Wash face twice daily

prescriptions.name: Sunscreen SPF 30+
prescriptions.sig: Apply daily before sun exposure

prescriptions.notes: Combination therapy with oral antibiotic and topical agents. Counsel on potential photosensitivity with doxycycline; strict sun protection is essential. Expect gradual improvement over 6–8 weeks; adherence to full 12-week course is important. Monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and skin irritation.

prescriptions.name: Melasma
prescriptions.summary: Melasma is an acquired hyperpigmentation disorder characterized by symmetric, blotchy brownish macules on sun-exposed areas, particularly the face. It is more common in females and darker skin types. Management involves photoprotection, topical depigmenting agents, and procedural therapies. Treatment is stepwise and requires long-term maintenance due to high recurrence rates.

prescriptions.name: Sunscreen SPF 50+ (tinted preferred)
prescriptions.sig: Apply daily, reapply every 2-3 hours (indefinite)

prescriptions.name: Hydroquinone 4% + Tretinoin 0.05% + Fluocinolone 0.01% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply thin layer to affected facial areas ONCE daily at bedtime (max 8 weeks)

prescriptions.name: Azelaic acid 15-20% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply twice daily (maintenance after stopping hydroquinone)

prescriptions.name: Kojic acid 2% / Tranexamic acid 3% serum
prescriptions.sig: Apply twice daily (alternative maintenance)

prescriptions.name: Tranexamic acid 250 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 8-12 weeks (refractory cases)

prescriptions.notes: Stepwise approach: Step 1 (all patients): SPF 50+ sunscreen + sun avoidance. Step 2 (first-line): Triple combination cream × 8 weeks. Step 3 (at 8 weeks): If improved → stop hydroquinone → start maintenance (azelaic acid/kojic acid). If not improved → add oral tranexamic acid 250 mg BID. Step 4 (at 12 weeks if inadequate): Consider PRP injections, gentle chemical peels, or low-fluence laser (dermatologist only). Step 5 (long-term): Maintenance cream + daily sunscreen + pulse hydroquinone courses as needed. Assess epidermal vs dermal vs mixed pattern using Wood's lamp. Strict photoprotection is critical for all patients.

prescriptions.name: Acute Cystitis (Pregnant Patient)
prescriptions.summary: Acute cystitis in pregnancy is a common bacterial infection of the bladder that requires prompt antibiotic treatment to prevent complications such as pyelonephritis and preterm labor. Asymptomatic bacteriuria also requires treatment in pregnancy. Antibiotic selection must consider fetal safety, with fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin as first-line options, avoiding nitrofurantoin near term. Urine culture is essential to guide therapy, and test-of-cure is recommended.

prescriptions.name: Fosfomycin trometamol 3g sachet
prescriptions.sig: Dissolve in 50-100 ml water. Take as a single dose NOW.

prescriptions.name: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule twice daily for 7 days (if fosfomycin unavailable; avoid at term 38-42 weeks)

prescriptions.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule four times daily for 7 days (second-line if nitrofurantoin contraindicated)

prescriptions.notes: LABORATORY: Urine culture (midstream) – send NOW; Test-of-cure urine culture 1-2 weeks after treatment completion. REFER IF: Fever >38°C, flank pain, no improvement after 48 hours, vomiting. Single-dose fosfomycin has the highest cure rate for acute cystitis. Nitrofurantoin is safe in pregnancy but contraindicated at term (38-42 weeks) due to risk of neonatal hemolysis. Cephalexin is a safe second-line option. Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy must also be treated. Hydration and urinary alkalinization may provide symptomatic relief. Consider admission for parenteral antibiotics if pyelonephritis suspected.

prescriptions.name: Acute Tonsillitis (Pregnant - Penicillin Allergy)
prescriptions.summary: Acute tonsillitis in pregnancy is an inflammatory infection of the palatine tonsils, commonly caused by group A Streptococcus (GAS). For penicillin-allergic pregnant patients without anaphylactic reaction, cephalexin is the first-line alternative. Erythromycin is the preferred macrolide in pregnancy due to extensive safety data. Azithromycin may be used if other options are unavailable. Supportive care with paracetamol, saline gargles, and hydration is essential. Monitor for complications and refer for suppurative complications or airway compromise.

prescriptions.name: Cephalexin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 capsule FOUR times daily (every 6 hours) for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

prescriptions.name: Erythromycin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet FOUR times daily for 7-10 days (Pregnancy Category B)

prescriptions.name: Azithromycin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet ONCE daily for 3 days (use only if cephalexin and erythromycin unavailable)

prescriptions.name: Paracetamol 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: As needed for pain/fever (safe in pregnancy)

prescriptions.name: Warm saline gargles
prescriptions.sig: 3 times daily for symptomatic relief

prescriptions.followUp: 5-7 days (if no improvement, consider throat swab and culture)
prescriptions.notes: EXPECTED OUTCOME: 24-48 hours: Significant symptom improvement; 7-10 days: Complete resolution. REFER IF: Difficulty breathing or stridor, inability to swallow saliva (drooling), muffled voice (hot potato voice), unilateral tonsillar swelling pushing uvula, fever >39°C for >48 hours, dehydration. Cephalexin is first-line for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy (safe, Category B). Erythromycin is the preferred macrolide in pregnancy with most documented experience. Azithromycin is not first-line for Strep pyogenes but can be used if other options unavailable. Emphasize rest and hydration. Consider throat swab for culture if no improvement at 5-7 days.

prescriptions.name: Scabies
prescriptions.summary: Scabies is a highly contagious parasitic infestation caused by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, characterized by intense nocturnal pruritus and burrows in interdigital spaces, wrists, and flexural areas. Diagnosis is clinical, with burrow identification and family history being key. Treatment involves topical permethrin 5% cream as first-line, with ivermectin for refractory or crusted cases. All household contacts must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfestation. Environmental decontamination is essential for cure.

prescriptions.name: Permethrin 5% cream
prescriptions.sig: Apply to entire body from neck to toes (including under nails, between fingers/toes, groin, buttocks, soles). Leave 8-12 hours. Wash off. Repeat after 7 days.

prescriptions.name: Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg
prescriptions.sig: Single dose (weight-based). Repeat after 7-14 days if needed (for refractory/crusted scabies).

prescriptions.name: Cetirizine 10 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 2-4 weeks (for itching)

prescriptions.followUp: 2 weeks (assess response), 4 weeks (if no improvement, reassess)
prescriptions.notes:
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Atopic dermatitis (no burrows, flexural distribution, less nocturnal itch); Papular urticaria (insect bites, no burrows); Contact dermatitis (exposure history, sharp borders); Pediculosis (lice visible); Prurigo nodularis (chronic, excoriated nodules).

ENVIRONMENTAL: Hot water wash (≥50°C/122°F) for bedding, clothes, towels; Seal non-washable items in plastic bag for 1 week; Vacuum carpets and furniture; Treat all household contacts simultaneously.

REFER IF: Crusted scabies, immunocompromised patient, no improvement after 2 cycles, secondary bacterial infection.

EXPECTED OUTCOME: Mites killed after 1st application; Pruritus resolves in 2-4 weeks; Complete cure after 2 applications (days 1 and 7-14).

KEY POINTS: All household contacts must be treated simultaneously regardless of symptoms. Permethrin is safe in pregnancy and children >2 months. Ivermectin is pregnancy category C. Pruritus may persist for 2-4 weeks due to hypersensitivity reaction even after successful treatment.

prescriptions.name: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
prescriptions.summary: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an infection of the upper female genital tract, including the uterus, fallopian tubes, and ovaries, typically caused by ascending organisms from the lower tract (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and anaerobic bacteria). Classic presentation includes bilateral lower abdominal pain, adnexal tenderness, cervical motion tenderness, fever, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential to prevent complications such as infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and chronic pelvic pain. Empiric broad-spectrum therapy covering gonorrhea, chlamydia, and anaerobes is recommended. Treatment should be initiated empirically in sexually active young women with pelvic pain and no other identifiable cause.

prescriptions.name: Ceftriaxone 1g IM
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Doxycycline 100 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole 400 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Levofloxacin 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Metronidazole 500 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 14 days

prescriptions.name: Moxifloxacin 400 mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 14 days (if M. genitalium suspected)

prescriptions.name: Cefoxitin 2g IM
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Probenecid 1g oral
prescriptions.sig: Single dose

prescriptions.name: Cefotetan 2g IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 12 hours (switch to oral doxycycline after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days

prescriptions.name: Cefoxitin 2g IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 6 hours (switch to oral doxycycline after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days

prescriptions.name: Clindamycin 900mg IV
prescriptions.sig: Every 8 hours (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

prescriptions.name: Gentamicin IV/IM
prescriptions.sig: 2mg/kg loading, then 1.5mg/kg every 8 hours (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

prescriptions.notes:
REGIMEN A (First-line - Cephalosporin-Based): Ceftriaxone 1g IM single dose + Doxycycline 100mg BID × 14 days + Metronidazole 400mg BID × 14 days.

REGIMEN B (Second-line - Fluoroquinolone-Based): 
- Option 1: Levofloxacin 500mg OD × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days
- Option 2: Moxifloxacin 400mg OD × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days (if M. genitalium suspected)

REGIMEN C (Third-line - Alternative): Cefoxitin 2g IM single dose + Probenecid 1g oral single dose + Doxycycline 100mg BID × 14 days + Metronidazole 500mg BID × 14 days.

REGIMEN D (Fourth-line - Parenteral/Hospital): 
- Option 1: Cefotetan 2g IV q12h OR Cefoxitin 2g IV q6h + Doxycycline 100mg BID (switch to oral after 24-48 hrs), total 14 days
- Option 2: Clindamycin 900mg IV q8h + Gentamicin 2mg/kg IV/IM loading then 1.5mg/kg IV/IM q8h (switch to oral doxycycline 100mg BID to complete 14 days)

PARTNERS: Treat all partners within 60 days.

REFER IF: No improvement after 72 hours, pregnancy, severe illness, tubo-ovarian abscess, or inability to tolerate oral medications.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: 
- Screen for HIV, syphilis, and other STIs
- Counsel on safe sex practices and contraception
- Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment completed and symptoms resolved
- Consider pregnancy test in all reproductive-age women
- Hospitalization criteria: pregnant, severe illness, suspected surgical emergency, tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate oral medications, or lack of response to outpatient therapy
- Test of cure not routinely recommended for chlamydia/gonorrhea unless symptoms persist or pregnancy
- Repeat testing for chlamydia/gonorrhea recommended in 3-6 months due to high reinfection rates
- Consider IUD removal if symptoms persist after 72 hours

prescriptions.name: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB-O - Ovulatory Dysfunction)
prescriptions.summary: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding (AUB) is a common gynecological condition characterized by irregular, heavy, or prolonged menstrual bleeding in the absence of structural pathology. In ovulatory dysfunction (AUB-O), bleeding results from anovulation or oligo-ovulation, leading to unopposed estrogen stimulation and endometrial instability. Diagnosis is clinical with normal pelvic exam and negative pregnancy test. Medical management focuses on controlling acute bleeding, regulating menstrual cycles, and preventing recurrence. The combination of tranexamic acid and combined oral contraceptives is highly effective, with tranexamic acid reducing blood loss by 40-60%.

prescriptions.name: Tranexamic Acid 500mg
prescriptions.sig: 1-2 tablets (500-1000mg) three times daily for 3-5 days during menses (reduces blood loss by 40-60%)

prescriptions.name: Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (ethinyl estradiol 30-35mcg + progestin)
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet daily for 3-6 months (regulates cycle, prevents recurrence)

prescriptions.name: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet twice daily for 3 months (treats iron deficiency anemia)

prescriptions.name: Folic Acid 5mg
prescriptions.sig: 1 tablet once daily for 3 months

prescriptions.name: Paracetamol 500mg
prescriptions.sig: As needed for dysmenorrhea (painful periods)

prescriptions.notes:
CLUES: Irregular heavy/prolonged bleeding + no structural cause + anovulatory pattern + normal pelvic exam + negative pregnancy test.

BEST SINGLE PRESCRIPTION (Highest Cure Rate): Tranexamic Acid 500mg - 1-2 tablets (500-1000mg) TID for 3-5 days during menses + Combined Oral Contraceptive Pill (ethinyl estradiol 30-35mcg + progestin) - 1 tablet daily for 3-6 months.

SUPPORTIVE THERAPY: Ferrous Sulfate 200mg BID for 3 months (treats iron deficiency anemia) + Folic Acid 5mg OD for 3 months + Paracetamol 500mg as needed for dysmenorrhea.

DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: Structural causes (fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis), coagulopathies, thyroid dysfunction, endometrial hyperplasia/malignancy, pregnancy complications, infection.

ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS:
- Rule out pregnancy with serum/urine hCG
- Evaluate for iron deficiency anemia with complete blood count and ferritin
- Consider pelvic ultrasound to exclude structural pathology
- Endometrial biopsy indicated in women >45 years or with risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, chronic anovulation, tamoxifen use)
- Lifestyle modifications: weight management if obese, regular exercise
- NSAIDs (mefenamic acid, ibuprofen) can also reduce menstrual blood loss by 20-30%
- Levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (Mirena) is an excellent long-term option for heavy menstrual bleeding
- If bleeding persists despite medical therapy, consider endometrial ablation or hysterectomy
- Screen for thyroid disorders and coagulopathies (von Willebrand disease) in appropriate patients
